title: Bubble and Squeak
subtitle: Fried potato and cabbage cakes
excerpt: The British way with leftover vegetables: mashed potato and cooked cabbage or Brussels sprouts fried in a pan until the outside is brown and crisp and the inside is soft. Excellent on its own for lunch, or alongside a fried egg and a rasher.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bubble and squeak takes its name from the sounds the vegetables make as they cook in the pan. It is one of the great examples of British cucina povera: a dish designed to use up leftover boiled or roast potatoes and cooked brassicas from a Sunday dinner or Christmas meal. Early recipes from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries included meat; the modern meatless version became standard by the mid-twentieth century. The name has also been used for a dish of fried boiled beef and cabbage. The defining characteristic is the crust: the high heat produces a golden, slightly charred exterior while the interior stays soft and yielding. It can be made as one large cake and served in wedges, or as individual patties.

content.text: The mixture must be as dry as possible. Wet mashed potato or waterlogged cabbage makes it difficult to form a crust. Leave the mixture pressed into the pan undisturbed for several minutes to build the crust before turning; flipping too soon breaks the cake.

items.preparation: cooked and mashed, or crushed leftover boiled potatoes
or Brussels sprouts; cooked and roughly chopped
finely diced; or use spring onions

content.text: Mix the mashed potato and chopped cabbage or sprouts together. Season generously with salt and pepper. The mixture should hold together when pressed.

Heat the butter and oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion for 3 minutes until softened. Add the potato and cabbage mixture and press firmly into the pan with a spatula to form a large cake. Cook over medium heat without moving for 8 to 10 minutes until a deep golden-brown crust has formed on the bottom.

To flip, slide the cake onto a plate, then invert back into the pan. Cook for a further 5 minutes until the second side is equally golden. Alternatively, break the cake into rough pieces as you cook for a more casual result with more caramelised edges. Serve hot.
